extraction.name: PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language
extraction.description: PIQA is a benchmark dataset for physical commonsense understanding framed as multiple choice question answering. Given a goal in natural language and two possible solutions, exactly one solution is correct. The dataset focuses on everyday situations with a preference for atypical solutions and is designed to evaluate whether language models capture physical commonsense knowledge.
extraction.creator: Yonatan Bisk; Rowan Zellers; Ronan Le Bras; Jianfeng Gao; Yejin Choi
extraction.publisher: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence
extraction.citeAs: Bisk, Yonatan; Zellers, Rowan; Le Bras, Ronan; Gao, Jianfeng; Choi, Yejin. PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. 2020.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was collected as goal-solution pairs for a multiple choice question answering task. Annotators were prompted with links to instructables.com and asked to glance at the instructions of an instructable and use it as inspiration to construct two component tasks. They articulated a physical goal, wrote a valid solution, and provided a permutation of their own solution that makes it invalid, often subtly. Annotators were seeded with instructables from six categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop. Additional qualification HITs were run before the main annotation stage and validation was performed afterwards by other annotators.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: User-generated content data, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The prompts were derived from instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for doing tasks such as cooking, car repair, crafting, and manipulating objects using everyday materials. Annotators used instructables links as inspiration for creating goal and solution pairs.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset was cleaned using the AFLite algorithm to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples. AFLite discarded instances whose feature representations were highly indicative of the target label. The train, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite. During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Examples were tokenized by SpaCy for statistics. The dataset was further cleaned of basic artifacts using AFLite. During model experiments, examples were truncated at 150 tokens, affecting 1% of the data.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were asked to provide 1) a physical goal, 2) a valid solution, and 3) a trick that should sound reasonable but be wrong, often due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. They were prompted with instructables to encourage creative, less prototypical uses of everyday objects. A qualification HIT containing well constructed and underspecified goal-solution pairs was used before participation in the main HIT, and annotators had to identify which were well formed with greater than 80% accuracy. Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness. During validation, examples with low agreement were removed. Human evaluation used majority vote, and annotators for that evaluation had to achieve at least 90% on the qualification HIT.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Examples with low agreement were removed during validation. This often removed correct examples that required expert-level domain knowledge and were judged outside commonsense. Human performance was calculated by majority vote. The interface included a diff button highlighting where the two solutions differ, which improved annotator accuracy and speed substantially.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper positions PIQA as a benchmark to advance language representations that capture physical commonsense knowledge useful beyond NLP, including for robots that interact with the world and understand natural language. The authors argue that learning about the world from language alone is limiting and that knowledge should eventually be learned from interaction with the world.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper discusses reporting bias as a major issue in physical commonsense text, noting that facts about everyday physical interactions are rarely directly reported. Early unconstrained prompts led annotators toward prototypical solutions and common tools from kitchens or garages, swamping the dataset with reporting bias. To address this, annotators were prompted with instructables to flatten the distribution of referenced objects. The dataset was also cleaned with AFLite to remove annotation artifacts and stylistic biases that could make labels predictable.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The paper notes that some development errors were actually correct but required a web search to verify. Examples requiring expert-level knowledge, such as special woodworking terminology, were removed during validation because they should not fall under commonsense. The authors also state that learning about the world from language alone is limiting, and that future systems might match humans on the dataset by finding large in-domain data and fine-tuning heavily, but that this is not the intended point of the benchmark.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is introduced as a benchmark for evaluating and studying physical commonsense understanding in natural language models. It is used with train, development, and test splits for model training, validation, and testing on multiple choice question answering.
